title: What happens after a recording arrives
description: Follow uploaded media through previews, analysis and workflows without confusing partial results with lost video.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional shop camera uploading a new clip. The team expects a playable video, a thumbnail and analysis at once. Is that one single operation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It's a chain of independent jobs. The Agent uploads to Vault and submits an event. Intake checks the account and device context, then later workers register the recording and contribute the information people see in Hub.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So a clip appearing before its thumbnail isn't automatically a failed upload?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. The source recording and its derived previews are different outputs. Registration makes the recording discoverable; thumbnail and sprite workers may finish later. Diagnose the missing piece instead of treating every incomplete card as lost video.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where do detections, tracks and useful counts come from?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Enabled analysis stages produce those structured results. They can support overlays, markers, Analytics and alerts. But that processing depends on the services and configuration actually enabled for the deployment.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: If we deploy a new stage today, does yesterday's entire archive suddenly gain those results?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Existing footage isn't automatically reprocessed simply because a model or stage was deployed. Check which recording and run you're inspecting before expecting a new result to appear.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How do workflows fit alongside the established processing pipeline?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They coexist. The event pipeline continues handling core intake and established services. Workflows add configurable stages with explicit run status, and a later stage can depend on an earlier result.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our operator sees a queued workflow and clicks Run again. Is that a harmless refresh?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It can create a separate run. Check the existing status before repeating the action. Results and downstream operations are asynchronous, so a queue or worker problem needs diagnosis rather than a growing collection of duplicate requests.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What must remain true as the recording passes between services?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Its organisation and project scope must stay with it. Background results belong with the source recording, not whichever workspace an operator happens to select later. Access and additional workflow permissions still apply.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And are all the derived results permanent?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They're tied to the source lifecycle unless a feature creates a separately managed copy, such as a case archive. For a useful first check, follow one recording from upload to its visible results and compare the stage status with what the operator sees.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
